How Washington property tax is set

In Washington the bill has two authors. Your county assessor decides what the parcel is worth; the county treasurer turns that into a statement and takes your payment. RCW 84.40.020 requires a fresh assessment every year, pegged to the January 1 date.

The standard, from RCW 84.40.030, is full market value, spelled in the statute as 100 percent of true and fair value in money. Residential assessors lean on comparable sales from the last five years and must honor current zoning, so the land cannot be valued for something the rules forbid. Land and buildings are valued apart, and the total cannot top today's worth of the property.

Whenever the assessor changes a value, notice must follow inside thirty days of the appraisal (RCW 84.40.045). The notice lists the former and new figures, with land and improvements apart, and briefly explains appeal rights. Nothing of this kind can be mailed from January 15 through February 15.

Due dates and penalties

Washington lets you split the bill: April 30 for the first installment, October 31 for the second. RCW 84.56.020 is the source, and splitting opens up once a parcel's bill reaches $50.

Payment or chargeDate or rate
First halfPay by April 30
Second halfPay by October 31
Tax statementsMailed by March 15 if budgets, levies and the tax roll are delivered on time
Interest on a house or small rental, up to four units9 percent per year, computed monthly from delinquency, with no penalty
Interest on other property12 percent per year
Penalties on nonresidential, larger multifamily and personal property3 percent on tax delinquent June 1, plus 8 percent more on December 1

A payment with an unreadable postmark, or one made through an automated check service, is still on time if it lands within three business days after the deadline. Some treasurers set up payment plans and accept part payments, which go to the oldest delinquent year unless you direct otherwise. Phone the treasurer to see what is offered.

How to appeal your assessment

Send your petition, on the state form, to the board of equalization in your county. RCW 84.40.038 gives you the latest of four possible dates:

  • The July 1 that falls in the assessment year.
  • Thirty days after the assessment or value change notice went in the mail.
  • Thirty days from the assessor emailing it or telling you it is online.
  • Any longer window the county adopts, up to sixty days.

Use the prescribed form and fill it out completely, because a petition that falls short may be refused. Lateness can be forgiven if you file within a reasonable time and have good cause. Illustrations in the statute: a death or serious illness in the family, absence from your mailing address for over fifteen of the allowed days when the deadline falls after July 1, wrong written advice from county staff, a flood or earthquake, and a postal delay on record. The board has no choice but to waive the deadline when your area was revalued, your own value held steady and you were never sent a revaluation notice.

You may skip the county board and go straight to the state Board of Tax Appeals, but only if you, the assessor and most of the county board agree to it. The state board can refuse, sending the case back to the county. Forms and a residential owner checklist are posted by the Board of Tax Appeals.

If a payment date arrives while your appeal is pending, call the treasurer about how to pay.

Property tax relief for homeowners

Relief comes in three forms here: an exemption, a deferral, and a grant that goes to the surviving spouse of a veteran. The Department of Revenue sets out the details on its exemptions and deferrals page, and your county assessor takes the applications.

  • Senior, disability and veteran exemption. The home must be your owned Washington primary residence, and your income must sit within the county limit. You also need to turn 61 by December 31 of the assessment year, be unable to work because of disability, or hold a qualifying VA rating as a veteran. Savings vary with income, home value and local levies. The assessor sets renewal timing, no less often than every six years.
  • Senior and disability deferral. Meant for owner-occupants aged 60 or more, or retired on disability, with equity enough to cover the state's interest. What you defer earns 5 percent simple interest, and repayment is triggered by a sale, the owner's death, or moving out of the house as a primary home.
  • Veteran's surviving spouse. This grant is never repaid so long as the recipient remains in the home through at least December 15 of the year it is received.

The collection statutes add two protections. If a property qualifies for deferral, the treasurer cannot sell it and instead requires a declaration to defer (RCW 84.64.050(6)). Separately, RCW 84.56.020(19) gives an income-qualified owner a one-time waiver of back interest and penalties when the home they live in is headed for tax foreclosure. The window opens about 60 days before the three-year point.

Income limits vary by county. Call the assessor for this year's figure before you decide to apply.

When property taxes go unpaid

Interest starts building on the delinquency date. Three years on, the county begins steps toward foreclosure. RCW 84.64.050 tells the treasurer to issue certificates of delinquency at that point and foreclose the tax liens in the county's name. The owner and every holder of a recorded interest are served, and each then has thirty days to respond or pay.

Before a sale the treasurer orders a title search to verify the legal description and who holds record title, and that person is treated as the owner when notices go out. No certificate can issue when the delinquency is $100 or less before interest and penalties, unless a local government has declared the parcel a nuisance.

Treasurers are also required to point delinquent owners toward help, including the statewide foreclosure hotline the Washington State Housing Finance Commission recommends. Around the two-year mark the treasurer shares the owner's contact details with a homeownership resource center or similar designated body.

Selling with taxes owed, and excise tax at closing

The lien for each year attaches on January 1, so the bill rides with the house until paid. If the contract is silent, RCW 84.60.020 puts the seller on the hook for the stretch of the year before the sale date and the buyer on the hook for what follows. Most contracts set their own split, and escrow applies it at closing. If back taxes are owed, request a payoff quote from the treasurer with interest through your closing day.

Selling also means paying real estate excise tax, which the Department of Revenue explains at its REET page. Sellers normally owe it, payment goes to the county treasurer by the date of sale, and what stays unpaid can turn into a lien. From January 1, 2027 the state share is 1.1 percent of the price up to $551,000, then 1.28 percent up to $1,551,000, 2.75 percent up to $3,051,000 and 3 percent beyond. A local rate sits on top, and unpaid tax draws interest after one month. Look for the final figure on your settlement statement.

Short on time, with taxes owed, repairs waiting or a tenant living there? A cash buyer can fold those into an as-is price. The payoff shows as its own line, so you can see what leaves your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to appeal my Washington property value?

Whichever is last: July 1, thirty days after the notice went out by mail or email, or a longer county window of up to sixty days. For good cause such as serious illness, a flood or a postal delay on record, the county board of equalization can excuse a late petition.

Can I pay Washington property tax in two payments?

Yes, once the parcel's bill is $50 or more. Half goes in by April 30 and the balance by October 31. Your treasurer may also allow a payment plan or partial payments.

How much interest do late Washington property taxes carry?

Homes and small rentals of up to four units owe 9 percent a year, figured monthly, and no penalty. Other property owes 12 percent. Nonresidential property, bigger multifamily buildings and personal property add a 3 percent penalty on June 1 and 8 percent more on December 1.

Do I have to pay property tax if I qualify for a senior exemption or deferral?

An exemption cuts the bill using your income, home value and levy rates. A deferral only postpones it, at 5 percent simple interest, until you sell, die or move out. Apply for either through the county assessor.

Who pays property tax at closing when I sell my house in Washington?

Whatever the sale agreement says. With no clause, the seller pays for the days before closing and the buyer pays for the remainder. Escrow normally does the math on the settlement statement next to the seller's excise tax.

What the Washington homestead exemption does

Chapter 6.13 of the Revised Code of Washington shields equity in your home from most unsecured creditors. The legislature put it that way in 2021, describing the purpose as protecting a homeowner's equity against unsecured creditors.

The protected amount applies to net value: market value minus liens and encumbrances that rank ahead of the judgment being collected. Your mortgage balance comes off first, and the exemption is measured on what is left. When a creditor holds a judgment against you, the exemption decides how much equity the creditor can reach and how much remains yours.

This is a creditor-protection rule, separate from property tax breaks for seniors or disabled owners, which the county assessor handles. A seller with a judgment, a lien or a bankruptcy in the background should sort out both questions before accepting an offer.

How much equity is protected

Under RCW 6.13.030 the exemption is the greater of $125,000 or the county median sale price for a single-family home in the preceding calendar year. In higher-priced counties the median usually wins, so the protection depends on where the house is.

Courts take the median from the Washington Center for Real Estate Research, or from a successor the Office of Financial Management designates if that center stops publishing. There is a third rule: when another state is trying to collect income tax on pension or retirement benefits earned while the owner lived in Washington, the homestead has no dollar limit.

  • Floor: $125,000 of net equity.
  • Higher-value counties: the prior year's county median single-family sale price, if larger.
  • Pension income tax judgments from another state: no dollar cap.

To find the median for your county, ask the court clerk or your attorney which published number the court is using.

Do you have to file to claim it?

Usually not. A home you occupy as your principal residence is protected automatically from the moment you move in, under RCW 6.13.040. A house qualifies, and so does a mobile home, whether or not it is permanently attached to the land, and so does land you own and mean to build on and live on.

A written declaration is needed only when you choose a homestead from land you do not yet occupy. The owner signs a declaration of homestead, acknowledged the way a deed is, and records it with the recording officer of the county where the land lies. It must say you live there or intend to, give the legal description and estimate the actual cash value.

If you already claim another parcel, you also record a declaration of abandonment for that one, stating the property is no longer your homestead, with the legal description and the abandonment date. The county auditor's recording office can tell you its format and fee.

Moving out or selling

Washington presumes you abandoned a homestead you have vacated for six months in a row. If you will be gone longer, have no other principal residence and do not mean to give the home up, RCW 6.13.050 lets you record a declaration of nonabandonment. It states that you intend to return, where you will live meanwhile, how long you expect to be away, the reason, and a description of the property.

A sale does not wipe out protection at once. Under RCW 6.13.070, proceeds from a voluntary, good-faith sale made in order to buy a new homestead stay exempt for one year from receipt, up to the statutory amount, and the new homestead bought with them is protected as well. Insurance money paid for a destroyed home gets the same one-year treatment if it is held to restore or replace the house.

If you plan to sell, rent for a while and then buy again, watch that one-year window. Keep the proceeds in an account you can trace, and talk to an attorney before spending them on anything but a replacement home.

Debts that can still reach a homestead

The exemption does not shield the house from every creditor. RCW 6.13.080 names debts that can be enforced against it whatever the protected amount.

  • Debts secured by mechanic's, laborer's, construction, material supplier's, vendor's, maritime or automobile repair liens on that property.
  • Debts secured by a security agreement covering the property, or by a mortgage or deed of trust signed and acknowledged by both spouses or both domestic partners, or by an unmarried owner.
  • Court-ordered child support and maintenance.
  • Medical assistance the state paid correctly on your behalf.
  • Condominium, homeowners' or common interest community association liens.
  • Sales and related taxes collected but not remitted to the Department of Revenue.

A first mortgage, a home equity loan you signed, a contractor's lien and unpaid association assessments all stay attached to the house and get paid or cleared at closing. The exemption mainly counts against unsecured judgment creditors such as credit card or medical collectors.

Judgment liens and a forced sale

A judgment against a homestead owner becomes a lien on the value above the exemption once the creditor records it with the county recording officer, under RCW 6.13.090. A Department of Revenue tax warrant becomes a lien when it is filed in superior court. If you have a recorded judgment, ask the closing agent how the lien will be paid off at closing.

A creditor who wants to force a sale goes through superior court. The creditor petitions for an appraiser, the owner gets at least ten days' notice of the hearing, and the appraiser reports within fifteen days of appointment. When the net value is above the exemption and the land can be divided without material injury, the court can set off the exempt portion to the owner. When it cannot, the court orders a sale at which no bid below the exemption amount can be accepted.

Sale money is paid in a fixed order: the homestead exemption to the owner first, then the creditor up to the execution amount, then any balance to the owner. Cash paid to you keeps the protection the home had.

What spouses and domestic partners must sign

Both spouses, or both state-registered domestic partners, must sign and acknowledge any deed or mortgage of a homestead under RCW 6.13.060. A power of attorney for conveying or encumbering the homestead is the allowed exception. A dependent who is not a spouse or partner need not sign.

When one spouse or partner is incompetent or disabled and no guardian has been appointed, the other can ask the superior court in the homestead's county for an order allowing a sale or mortgage. The statute calls for a sworn petition filed thirty days before the hearing and notice by publication once a week for three weeks. After the order is entered, the sale has the same effect as if the applicant owned the property outright.

Sellers in this spot should build the court timeline into the closing date.

Homestead rules at a glance

TopicWashington rule
Protected amountGreater of $125,000 or prior-year county median single-family sale price
FilingAutomatic for an occupied principal residence; declaration only for land not yet occupied
AbandonmentPresumed after six continuous months away
Sale proceedsExempt for one year when used for a new homestead
Judgment lienAttaches to value above the exemption when recorded

Frequently asked questions

Is the Washington homestead exemption the same as a property tax exemption?

No. The exemption in chapter 6.13 RCW protects home equity from creditors. Property tax relief for seniors, disabled owners and others is a separate program through the county assessor.

Does a Washington homestead protect my home from foreclosure by my mortgage lender?

No. Under RCW 6.13.080 the exemption is unavailable against a mortgage or deed of trust signed by both spouses or partners, or by an unmarried owner, so the lender can still enforce its lien.

Can I keep the money if I sell my homestead?

Yes, within limits. Proceeds of a good-faith voluntary sale made to buy a new homestead stay exempt for one year from receipt, up to the statutory amount, and the replacement home is protected too.

What if I rent the house out or leave for more than six months?

A homestead is presumed abandoned after six months away in a row. If you mean to return and have no other principal residence, record a declaration of nonabandonment with the county before the gap grows.

Does the homestead amount change from county to county?

Yes. The floor is $125,000, but when the prior calendar year's county median single-family sale price is higher, that figure applies.

Washington estate tax and an inherited house

Washington does tax what a person leaves behind once the estate is larger than the exclusion amount, and a house counts toward the total. The tax falls on the estate as a whole, not on each heir's share, and the estate is itself a taxpayer under RCW 83.100.020.

If you inherited a house and plan to sell it, three questions matter: does the estate owe, does it have to file a return, and has the state released its claim on the property. All three turn on the date of death, so write that date down first.

Exclusion amount by date of death

The size of the exclusion depends on when the person died. RCW 83.100.020 sets $2,193,000 for deaths on or after July 1, 2018 and before July 1, 2025. For deaths from July 1, 2025 up to January 1, 2026 the figure is $3,000,000. It is $3,076,000 for January 1 through June 30, 2026, and $3,000,000 again for deaths on or after July 1, 2026.

An inflation formula starts with deaths in 2027. If the death came in 2027 or later, ask the Department of Revenue which amount applies.

People who lived in another state can be pulled in as well. An out-of-state owner of Washington real estate or tangible personal property may owe, and the tax on that estate is scaled down by a fraction based on how much of the gross estate sits here.

Tax rates

Rates are graduated and begin at 10 percent. For deaths on or after July 1, 2026, RCW 83.100.040 applies the schedule below to the Washington taxable estate, which is the gross estate minus allowed deductions and the exclusion amount.

Washington taxable estateInitial taxRate on the excess
$0 to $1,000,000$010%
$1,000,000 to $2,000,000$100,00014%

$6,000,000 to $7,000,000$910,00019%

Does the estate have to file a return?

Often yes. RCW 83.100.050 requires a Washington return whenever the gross estate equals or exceeds the exclusion amount, and that is true even if the tax works out to zero. An estate under the threshold files nothing.

Married couples get one carve-out. No return is needed if the decedent left a surviving spouse, the qualifying family residence passed to that spouse, no election calls for a return, and the gross estate minus the value of that residence is under the exclusion amount. The statute defines the qualifying family residence as the principal home of the marital community or domestic partnership on the date of death.

  • The threshold test uses the gross estate, which counts assets held outright or in trust wherever they are located.
  • Residents, and nonresidents who own Washington real property, can both be required to file.
  • The date of death controls, so a death in early 2026 uses different figures than one in late 2026.

Due dates, penalties and where to send the return

The return and the payment are both due nine months after the date of death. A request for extension and an estimated payment are due the same day. The state allows a six-month extension to file, but more time to file is not more time to pay, and tax unpaid after nine months accrues interest daily.

Filing late can add a penalty under RCW 83.100.070: 5 percent of the tax for each month the return is late, capped at the lesser of 25 percent of the tax or $1,500. Return the paperwork voluntarily before the department sends written notice and there is no penalty. The interest rate resets each January.

You can file and pay through My DOR or mail the return to the Department of Revenue, PO Box 47474, Olympia, WA 98504-7474. The estate tax examiners are at 360-704-5906 or estates@dor.wa.gov.

The state's claim and your closing

What ties the estate tax to a home sale is the state's claim against estate property. Under RCW 83.100.080 the department issues a release once the tax is paid, and after that the property is free of the state's claim for the tax. If the estate is big enough to owe, ask the department how to get the release before you list, so the closing is not held up.

Cash timing matters too. With payment due nine months after death and the house as the main asset, talk to the estate's attorney about selling first and paying from the proceeds. A cash buyer can help when the deadline is close, since the sale does not depend on a lender.

A practical order of work for heirs who want to sell:

  • Confirm the date of death and compare the gross estate to the exclusion amount for that date.
  • If a return is required, mark the nine-month due date on the calendar and plan the payment.
  • Ask the department how to obtain the release of the state's claim on the property.
  • Gather the death certificate and the court letters so the treasurer can process the deed paperwork at closing.

Excise tax when you inherit and when you sell

Getting the house by will or inheritance carries no real estate excise tax under WAC 458-61A-202, and a mortgage on the property does not change that. The county treasurer where the house sits receives the paperwork, which might be a certified death certificate, letters testamentary or letters of administration for a probated estate, or a signed lack of probate affidavit when no probate is opened.

A later sale is a different event. A transfer from an heir to an outside buyer is taxed, and the rule's example has an heir selling an inherited house for $50,000 and owing tax on all $50,000. If one heir pays the siblings to take sole title, tax is due on the amount paid, which is $120,000 in the rule's example.

For income tax, the basis of inherited property follows IRS Publication 551 rather than a simple purchase cost. Get that figure from a tax preparer before you set a price.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Washington estate tax exclusion for 2026?

$3,076,000 for deaths from January 1 through June 30, 2026, and $3,000,000 for deaths on or after July 1, 2026. RCW 83.100.020 sets both.

What is the top Washington estate tax rate?

For deaths on or after July 1, 2026 it is 20 percent on the taxable estate above $9,000,000. For deaths from July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2026 it is 35 percent above that same line.

When is the Washington estate tax return due?

Nine months after the date of death. You can get six more months to file, yet the tax itself is still due at nine months and interest builds daily on whatever is unpaid.

Do I owe real estate excise tax when I inherit a house in Washington?

No, inheriting by will is not taxed. If the heir later sells to a buyer, that sale is taxed on the full price.

Can an estate file a Washington return when no tax is owed?

Yes, and it must if the gross estate meets or exceeds the exclusion amount, even when the tax is zero. Smaller estates file nothing, and a narrow exception covers a family residence passing to a surviving spouse.

Washington real estate excise tax rates

Washington charges a graduated state excise tax on each sale of real property. It starts at 1.1 percent of the selling price and rises to 3 percent on the top slice. The rates come from RCW 82.45.060. Each rate applies only to the part of the price inside its band, so a sale is never taxed at 2.75 percent across the board.

The dollar thresholds are adjusted every fourth year. The Department of Revenue shows one set of band limits for sales through the end of 2026 and a new set for sales beginning January 1, 2027, so a closing in December 2026 and one in January 2027 use different numbers.

Land classified as agricultural land or timberland is taxed at a flat 1.28 percent state rate instead. The county assessor assigns that classification, and the buyer must state that the land will keep qualifying use.

Who pays, and by when

The seller owes it. RCW 82.45.080 puts the burden on the seller, with the buyer picking up the bill only if the seller skips it. Payment goes to the treasurer of the house's county on the sale date, regardless of when the deed gets recorded.

The sale date is the day the deed is signed and handed to the buyer or the buyer's agent. The Department of Revenue reads that as the notarization date unless someone shows otherwise. Timing matters because of these rules in RCW 82.45.100:

  • Tax not paid within one month of the sale starts to carry interest from the date of sale.
  • A penalty of 5 percent applies after one month, 10 percent after two months and 20 percent after three months.
  • The penalties can be collected from the seller only.
  • If the tax is late, the buyer is personally liable unless a document showing the sale is recorded in the county's property records.

Interest runs at 6 percent for both 2026 and 2027. Escrow normally deducts the tax from your proceeds, which is why few sellers ever mail a check themselves.

Local tax

Yes. Local tax is figured separately and stacked on the graduated state rate. Under RCW 82.46.010, a county or city may impose a tax of up to 0.25 percent of the selling price, and may impose an additional tax of up to 0.5 percent in lieu of a different local option listed in RCW 82.14.030(2).

The local rate follows the location code of the property, and the code can differ between an incorporated city and the unincorporated county around it. Get the exact combined rate from the county treasurer or escrow before you fix a net-proceeds figure. Local revenue pays for capital projects such as streets, parks and water and sewer systems.

Exemptions

The exemption list is short, and a transfer can use just one. Enter the code in section 7 of the affidavit and hold on to the documents behind it. Chapter 458-61A of the Washington Administrative Code has the details. Homeowners run into these most:

  • Inheritance or devise. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts transfers by will or inheritance, with or without a mortgage attached. A later sale by the heir is taxable on the full price. An heir who buys out siblings with cash owes tax on that cash.
  • Gifts. Under WAC 458-61A-201, a gift with no consideration is not a sale. If the person receiving the house takes over the mortgage payments, that counts as consideration and the debt is taxed. Both parties sign a supplemental statement.
  • Foreclosure transfers. WAC 458-61A-208 exempts trustee's sales, court-ordered mortgage foreclosure sales, sheriff's sales on a judgment, and deeds in lieu of foreclosure when no extra consideration passes.
  • Condemnation. A sale to a government under written notice of eminent domain is exempt under WAC 458-61A-206.
  • Bankruptcy. Transfers by a trustee after a confirmed chapter 11 or 12 plan are exempt under WAC 458-61A-207.

An ordinary arm's-length sale of a house, including a sale of an inherited or distressed house, fits none of these. It is taxed on the full selling price.

Filing the affidavit

The excise tax affidavit, the deed and the payment all go to the county treasurer where the property lies. Sending them to the state Department of Revenue instead can hold things up and lead to penalties and interest. Download forms from the Department's website.

Which form you need depends on the parcels. A single location affidavit covers one or more parcels inside one local jurisdiction code. A multiple locations affidavit with a worksheet is needed when parcels sit in different jurisdiction codes, even inside one county. An agent for the seller or buyer can sign it, and electronic signatures count when proper authentication is used.

Keep records that support the price and any exemption for at least four years. All sales are subject to audit, and under RCW 82.45.100 the Department generally can't assess or refund more than four years after the sale unless there was fraud, a misstatement of a material fact or a failure to report the sale. A refund request is also due within four years and goes through the county treasurer for a deeded transfer.

Consequences of nonpayment

Unpaid tax can become a lien on the property, and the state has two ways to collect from the seller. Under RCW 82.45.080 the Department of Revenue may bring an action of debt against the seller, or may proceed the way a lender would in a mortgage foreclosure, and using one route doesn't rule out the other. The Department also audits transactions after the fact and assesses additional tax with interest and penalties if a price was understated or an exemption was claimed without support.

Controlling interest transfers have their own rule. When 50 percent or more of an entity that owns Washington real estate changes hands within 36 months, the Department treats it as a sale of the real property, and the return is due within five days of the transfer. Anyone selling a house held in an LLC or partnership should call the Department's REET team before moving ownership interests.

Before and after closing

Ask escrow for a written estimate of state and local excise tax so the number appears on your settlement statement. Pin down the sale date, because the one-month clock starts on it. Claiming an exemption? Have the paper ready: letters testamentary or a death certificate for an inheritance, or the signed supplemental statement for a gift. Afterward, confirm the affidavit reached the county treasurer and file your copy. A cash sale taxes the same way. Closings tend to be faster, so the deduction from your proceeds simply happens sooner.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays the Washington excise tax, buyer or seller?

The seller. The buyer becomes liable only if the seller doesn't pay. Escrow usually subtracts the tax from your proceeds and forwards it to the county treasurer.

How is the state tax figured on a higher-priced home?

Rates stack by band. The first slice of the price is taxed at 1.1 percent, the next at 1.28 percent, and higher slices at higher rates. Local tax goes on top, so ask the treasurer or escrow for the final amount.

Do I owe the tax when I give a house to a relative?

Not for a true gift with no payment or debt assumed. Both sides sign a supplemental statement. If the relative begins paying your mortgage, the Department of Revenue counts that debt as consideration and taxes it.

When do penalties begin?

Payment is due on the sale date. Once a month passes, interest runs back to that date, and penalties of 5, 10 and 20 percent hit at one, two and three months. Only the seller is charged the penalties.

Does an inherited house trigger the tax?

No. Passing by will or inheritance is exempt, even with a mortgage attached. When the heir later sells, that sale is taxed on the full price. A death certificate or letters testamentary back up the claim.

Selling a house and the capital gains tax

A house closing does not set off Washington's capital gains excise tax. RCW 82.87.050 exempts land and buildings that pass by deed, real estate contract, judgment or a similar instrument filed as a public record where the property is located. Real estate is the first asset on the state's exemption list.

The tax itself, found in RCW 82.87.040, is 7 percent of an individual's Washington capital gains, plus another 2.90 percent on the portion above $1,000,000 from January 1, 2025. Only individuals pay it. If you also sold stock or a business interest in the same year, those sales can still be taxed. The house closing stays outside the chapter.

Which real estate sales are exempt?

An ordinary house sale moves title by deed, so it fits the exemption. So does a sale where you carry the financing, because the statute names a real estate contract. If you hold an interest in a privately owned company and sell it, only the part of your gain that comes from real estate the company owns directly is exempt.

  • Depreciable property under federal tax law has its own exemption.
  • Assets in a 401(k), 403(b), IRA or similar retirement account are exempt.
  • Timber, timberland, some livestock and commercial fishing privileges are exempt too.

Rates, deductions and credits for other assets

Before the rate applies, the state subtracts a standard deduction. RCW 82.87.060 sets it at $250,000 per individual, or $250,000 combined for spouses and domestic partners, adjusted for inflation. The adjusted figure is $270,000 for 2024 and $278,000 for 2025.

Gain from selling a qualified family-owned small business and certain charitable gifts can be deducted as well. If another state or country taxed the same gain, a credit applies, limited to the smaller of the Washington tax on those assets or the tax paid elsewhere. Losses do not carry forward into later years.

Tax featureAmount or rule
Base rate on Washington capital gains7%
Added rate on gains above $1,000,0002.90% from January 1, 2025
Standard deduction, 2025$278,000 per individual or couple
House sold by recorded deedExempt

Real estate excise tax (REET) when you sell

The Washington tax that does touch a home sale is REET, short for real estate excise tax. It applies to all real property sales unless a particular exemption fits. Sellers customarily cover it. When they skip it, the buyer picks up the obligation, and the debt may attach to the house as a lien.

Pay it to the treasurer in the county of the property. The clock starts on the date of sale, which means the notarization date of the deed, not the later recording date. One month past that date, penalty and interest begin. Send the treasurer the affidavit, the deed and the payment together.

The state portion is graduated. Sales beginning January 1, 2027 use these tiers:

  • 1.1 percent on the part of the price up to $551,000.
  • 1.28 percent on the part from $551,000 to $1,551,000.
  • 2.75 percent on the part from $1,551,000 to $3,051,000.
  • 3.0 percent on the part above $3,051,000.

Local REET is added on top. Farmland and timberland carry a flat 1.28 percent state rate. If you close before January 1, 2027, phone the treasurer's office for the thresholds in force and the local rate in your city.

Federal tax on the gain

Plenty of sellers end up owing no federal tax at all. A single filer can shield up to $250,000 of profit on a main home, and joint filers up to $500,000. Two tests apply. You had to own the home, and also live in it, for at least 24 months out of the 5 years ahead of closing. Those months need not line up, and the shield is generally unavailable if you used it on another sale in the previous two years.

Reporting and owing are different questions. If the closing agent sends you a Form 1099-S, the sale goes on your return even when every dollar of gain is covered. The same goes when part of the gain is not covered. Use Form 8949 and Schedule D where required, with IRS Publication 523 for worksheets.

Your gain equals the sale price minus adjusted basis. Basis begins at your purchase cost and grows by value-adding improvements. A gifted or inherited home follows different basis rules, covered in Publication 551, so an inherited house may start from a figure far from what the family once paid.

Return and payment dates for the state tax

When other assets do create a state bill, the return falls due on the same day as your federal income tax return, and filing is online through My DOR with the federal return attached. You can get more time to file only if a federal extension is already in hand and you ask the state for one in My DOR by April 15. More time to file never means more time to pay.

The payment deadline is usually April 15, moving to the next business day if that is a weekend or holiday. Starting with tax year 2026 you can prepay as early as six months before it is due. Late filing and late payment add penalties and interest, and paying under 80 percent of what you owe is a substantial underpayment that adds another penalty. Once you ask for an extension or send a payment, a return is required even if the tax comes to zero.

Planning the sale around these taxes

Begin with the closing date. REET runs off the whole selling price, so work out your price tier before accepting an offer and get the combined state and local number from the treasurer or closing agent. Hold on to the paperwork supporting the price and any exemption for at least four years, since Revenue may audit any transaction.

Next, set the house apart from other things you sold during the year. A deeded house is outside the capital gains tax, but shares of stock or a business stake may be inside it. Your tax preparer can total those and apply the deduction. Finally, work through the federal side: purchase and move-in dates, improvements, and depreciation if you rented out part of the home.

Inherited homes, houses with missed payments and houses needing costly repairs are taxed the same way as any other. A cash sale can spare you showings and repair requests, yet the excise tax still comes due. Before signing a contract with a price on it, call the Department of Revenue, the treasurer or a tax professional.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Washington capital gains tax on selling a primary residence?

No. RCW 82.87.050 exempts real estate that changes hands by recorded deed, so the state capital gains excise tax stays out of a house closing. REET is a separate tax that still applies, and federal gain rules run on their own track.

Who pays the real estate excise tax in Washington?

Usually the seller. When the seller leaves it unpaid, the buyer is on the hook and a lien can follow. Payment goes to the treasurer in the property's county.

How much of my home sale gain can I exclude on my federal return?

A single filer can exclude up to $250,000 and joint filers up to $500,000, provided the ownership and use tests are met. That means 24 months of owning and living there within the last 5 years.

What is the Washington capital gains tax rate?

Seven percent of Washington capital gains for an individual, with 2.90 percent more on the slice over $1,000,000 starting January 1, 2025. The standard deduction comes off first and is $278,000 for 2025.

When is the real estate excise tax due on a Washington house sale?

The sale date sets the due date, and that is the day the deed is notarized. Penalty and interest start once a month goes by with the tax unpaid.

The five stages of a Washington eviction

An eviction here is a court case called unlawful detainer. It runs through five stages: written notice, a summons and complaint in superior court, a hearing, a judgment, and a writ of restitution that puts the landlord back in possession. No stage can be skipped. An owner who removes a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 faces a wrongful eviction claim.

Each stage adds time, and each gives the tenant rules to rely on, so an owner planning to sell a rented house should map the dates before listing.

StageWhat happens
NoticeWritten notice served: 14 days for unpaid rent, 10 days for other lease breaches
Summons and complaintTenant is given a deadline to respond in writing
HearingCourt hears answers and defenses and may order a writ
JudgmentPossession is restored, with rent, damages and costs
Writ of restitutionSuperior court clerk issues it, with a bond if it comes before judgment

Filing the case and the summons

When the notice period ends without payment or a fix, the landlord files in superior court and has a summons served. RCW 59.18.365 supplies the form. It sets a response deadline of 5:00 p.m. on a stated date and warns that calling the landlord or the landlord's lawyer is not a response.

A tenant can answer with a notice of appearance, which is a letter saying the tenant is appearing in the case. It names the landlords and tenants and gives the tenant's name, a mailing address for legal papers, a signature, a phone number if any, and the case number if one has been assigned. Mailed responses must go out three days before the deadline. Hand-delivered or faxed ones are timely if they arrive by the deadline itself.

A tenant who responds is told of a hearing date in an order to show cause. One who ignores the notice and skips the hearing can be evicted, and the landlord may seek additional money. A tenant who moves out before the court date is asked by the summons to tell the landlord.

The show cause hearing

At the hearing on the landlord's motion for a writ, the tenant or anyone in possession may answer out loud or in writing and raise any legal or equitable defense or set-off arising from the tenancy. The judge questions the parties and witnesses to decide whether the landlord is entitled to possession. The procedure is in RCW 59.18.380.

If the landlord shows a right to possession, the court orders a writ of restitution returnable ten days after its date and sets the remaining issues for trial in the usual way. If not, the writ is denied and trial follows within thirty days. In a nonpayment case, a tenant has three days after being served with a pre-judgment writ to stay it by paying all rent found due, then paying monthly rent while the case goes on.

Before a writ issues ahead of final judgment, the landlord posts a bond in an amount the court sets. The bond covers costs and damages if the writ was wrongly obtained. Under RCW 59.12.090 the superior court clerk issues the writ, and it is returnable in twenty days.

Judgment and getting the tenancy back

If the landlord wins at trial, RCW 59.18.410 directs a judgment restoring the premises and, for rent or lease defaults, declaring the tenancy forfeited. The court also awards damages tied to the tenancy and rent found due. Late fees count only when the lease provides for them, and they are capped at $75 in total. Statutory costs and reasonable attorneys' fees may be added under RCW 59.18.290.

In a rent case, execution waits five court days after judgment. During that window, and before judgment, the tenant or another interested party can pay the rent due, court costs, allowed late fees and any awarded attorneys' fees and be restored to the tenancy. A tenant holding a pledge letter of financial assistance from a government or nonprofit agency gets until the eviction date. Anyone reinstated after judgment during the past 12 months pays an extra $50 for each time.

Can a court delay the writ?

After a nonpayment judgment, yes, within limits. A court may stay the writ for good cause on fair terms, but never for longer than 90 days from the order. The tenant carries the burden of proof, and the judge weighs listed factors.

  • Whether the default was willful or came from circumstances outside the tenant's control that are unlikely to repeat.
  • The tenant's ability to pay the judgment on time, and the payment history.
  • Whether the tenant otherwise substantially complies with the lease.
  • The hardship an eviction would cause, and conduct tied to other notices in the past six months.

A stay comes with a payment plan, and the first payment of one month's rent is due within five court days of the order. If the tenant misses a later payment, the landlord can serve a notice of default and the tenant then has three calendar days to leave before the sheriff may carry out the writ. A tenant who received three or more pay or vacate notices in the prior twelve months cannot seek this relief unless a notice was invalid. The court may also make a finding on whether the landlord can apply to the state landlord mitigation program.

How an eviction affects selling a rented house

It sets your timeline. When the sale is the reason you want the tenant out, RCW 59.18.650 calls for at least 90 days' written notice for a single-family residence, and you are expected to make reasonable attempts to sell, including listing the home, within 30 days after the tenant leaves. A fixed-term lease cannot be shortened on that ground without the tenant's written consent and at least 60 days to vacate.

The tenant has support, too. The court must appoint an attorney for an indigent tenant in an eviction case, subject to available funding. The statutory notices direct tenants to the Eviction Defense Screening Line, the Northwest Justice Project CLEAR hotline and free or low-cost mediation through dispute resolution centers, which can happen before any case is filed.

If you would rather not run the process yourself, talk with a Washington landlord-tenant attorney or the superior court clerk in your county about filing steps and fees. Ask the county treasurer what taxes are due at closing. A cash buyer can also take a house with a tenant dispute as is, and the settlement statement shows what is paid from proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Washington eviction take?

It varies. The notice runs 14 days for unpaid rent or 10 days for other breaches, then the tenant gets a response deadline on the summons and the court sets a hearing. A stay of up to 90 days can add time after a nonpayment judgment.

Can a Washington landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. Removing a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 makes the landlord liable for wrongful eviction, with damages of the greater of actual loss or three times the monthly rent, plus fees. The landlord has to use the court process and the writ of restitution.

Who carries out a writ of restitution in Washington?

The superior court clerk issues the writ and the sheriff executes it. The sheriff waits until the required court days or calendar days run out.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent?

In a nonpayment case, often yes. Before judgment or within five court days after it, the tenant can pay the rent due, costs, allowed late fees and awarded attorneys' fees and be restored to the tenancy. A pledge of rental assistance extends the time.

Does a tenant have a right to a lawyer in a Washington eviction?

An indigent tenant is entitled to a court-appointed attorney, subject to available funding. Qualifying income is at or below 200 percent of the federal level, and receipt of listed public benefits also qualifies.

What a quitclaim deed does in Washington

A Washington quitclaim deed hands over whatever rights the grantor holds on the day of signing, and nothing beyond that. Under RCW 64.04.050, a properly executed deed in the statutory quitclaim form is a good conveyance, release and quitclaim to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns of all the grantor's then existing legal and equitable rights in the described premises.

The same section sets a limit with real consequences: the deed does not reach after-acquired title unless words are added saying that is intended. If the grantor later gains a better claim to the land, the deed does not pick it up on its own.

The statutory form is short. It names the grantor and place of residence, states the consideration, says the grantor conveys and quitclaims to the grantee all interest in the described real estate, names the county and Washington as the state, and carries a date. Unlike a warranty deed, it makes no promises about title, so the buyer is relying on what the grantor actually owns.

What makes the deed valid?

Under RCW 64.04.020, every Washington deed must be in writing, signed by the person bound by it, and acknowledged before someone authorized to take acknowledgments. Every grantor has to be at the signing, so line up the notary before anyone travels.

For most family and cleanup transfers the working steps look like this:

  • Get the exact legal description from the last recorded deed or from the county auditor.
  • Find the assessor's parcel number, which belongs on the first page.
  • Have every grantor sign in front of a notary.
  • Complete the real estate excise tax affidavit, covered below.
  • Take the deed and affidavit to the county where the land sits and record it.

If the grantor is married or in a registered domestic partnership, ask a Washington attorney whether the spouse or partner must sign.

Recording the deed

You record with the county auditor in the county where the property is located. RCW 65.04.030 lists deeds, grants and transfers of real property among the instruments the auditor must record once fees are paid. RCW 65.04.045 fixes the first-page layout, so build that page carefully.

First-page elementRequirement
MarginsAt least three inches at the top, one inch on the bottom and sides
Return addressName and address for return, top left
Document titleImmediately below the three-inch margin
PartiesNames of grantors and grantees
Legal descriptionAbbreviated: lot, block, plat, or section, township, range and quarter section
Parcel numberAssessor's tax parcel or account number, set apart from other text

Pages can be no larger than 14 inches long and 8.5 inches wide, with type of eight point or larger and ink that images clearly. No attachments are allowed except firmly attached bar code or address labels. Apart from documents from governmental agencies, the deed may not contain a Social Security number, a date of birth tied to a person, or a parent's maiden name tied to a person.

Recording fees

The base fee is $5 for the first page and $1 for each added page of 8.5 by 14 inches or less, under RCW 36.18.010. That statute adds surcharges on every recorded instrument: $3 for the state library operations account, $2 for the library-archives building account while its financing contract is unpaid, a modernization surcharge, and further assessments set elsewhere.

With those add-ons, your receipt will show more than $5. Call the county auditor's recording office for the full fee at your page count, and ask whether it takes deeds by mail, at the counter or electronically.

The auditor's fee is separate from the real estate excise tax, which goes to the county treasurer, so expect two payments when you submit the deed.

Does a quitclaim deed trigger excise tax?

Often it does, unless an exemption applies. The Department of Revenue's real estate excise tax page explains that an affidavit is generally required whenever title passes by deed, grant, assignment or quitclaim. The tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, recorded or not. The date of sale is the date the deed is executed and delivered, which the department treats as the notarization date.

A true gift is the most common exemption. Under WAC 458-61A-201, a gift of real property is not a sale because nothing is given in return. Several traps follow from that rule:

  • If the new owner agrees to take over the mortgage, the debt is consideration and tax is due on it, though equity can still be gifted.
  • If the new owner starts making payments on the debt after the transfer, tax can be due on the debt being paid.
  • A refinance involving the new owner within six months of the transfer is presumed to make the transfer a sale. After six months, the presumption runs toward a gift.
  • Both grantor and grantee must sign a supplemental statement that goes with the affidavit, and the grantor must keep records in case of audit.

Other exemptions cover moving a home into a revocable trust and taking it back out without payment, and a deed between the same owners that only changes how they hold title, such as tenants in common becoming joint tenants (WAC 458-61A-211). Only one exemption may be claimed per transfer.

When a quitclaim is the wrong tool for selling

It is the wrong tool whenever the buyer needs reliable title. The deed gives over only what the grantor has, so a buyer who pays real money for a quitclaim gets no statement in the paper that the title is good. For an arm's-length sale, ask a Washington title company or attorney what the closing will need.

A quitclaim suits transfers among people who already trust each other, such as adding or removing a spouse after a divorce, placing a home in a revocable trust, or clearing a possible claim from an old record. If the house is in probate, the nonintervention powers in RCW 11.68.090 or a transfer on death deed may be the cleaner path.

If you need to sell a home with title questions, back taxes or heirs who disagree, a cash buyer can review the situation as is. Bring the last recorded deed and any court papers so the closing agent can see what needs to be cleared.

Frequently asked questions

Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title in Washington?

No. It passes only the grantor's then existing legal and equitable rights, and it does not reach after-acquired title unless the deed says so (RCW 64.04.050). A buyer who wants assurance about title usually asks for more than a quitclaim.

Who records a Washington quitclaim deed?

The county auditor where the property sits. The deed must be signed and acknowledged, and its first page needs the return address, title, parties, abbreviated legal description and assessor's parcel number.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Washington?

The statutory base is $5 for the first page and $1 for each additional page, plus several surcharges on every recorded instrument. Ask the county auditor for the total at your page count, and plan on a separate excise tax payment to the county treasurer.

Is a quitclaim deed between family members tax free in Washington?

It can be, if it is a true gift with no consideration. Assuming the mortgage, paying on the debt after the transfer, or refinancing with the new owner within six months can turn it into a taxable sale. Both parties sign a supplemental statement filed with the affidavit.

Can I use a quitclaim deed to leave my house to someone at my death?

Not as a death transfer. A quitclaim conveys the grantor's existing rights now. Washington's transfer on death deed under chapter 64.80 RCW is the recordable deed that takes effect at the owner's death, and it must be recorded with the county auditor before the owner dies.

How a Washington TOD deed works

A TOD deed lets a Washington owner pick who inherits a house without probate for that parcel, and without giving up any control in the meantime. Chapter 64.80 RCW, the state's uniform real property transfer on death act, creates the tool. RCW 64.80.020 lets one person name one or more beneficiaries who take at the owner's death.

Lawyers call the deed nontestamentary (RCW 64.80.040). That means it isn't a will, yet signing or revoking one takes the same mental capacity a will does (RCW 64.80.050). Deeds signed before June 12, 2014 are covered if the owner dies on or after that day (RCW 64.80.901). Other estate planning methods stay available (RCW 64.80.902).

What the deed needs to be valid

Think of it as a regular deed with one extra sentence, filed while you are still alive. RCW 64.80.060 lists three musts:

  • Everything a normal recordable lifetime deed requires.
  • Language saying the beneficiary receives the property when the owner dies.
  • Recording with the auditor in the county where the land sits, before the owner's death.

Signing alone isn't enough. A deed left in a drawer fails the recording rule. The county will also look at the usual first-page layout for recorded papers: three inches of blank space at the top, a return address, a title, the names of grantor and grantee, a short legal description and the assessor's parcel number (RCW 65.04.045). Your beneficiary needn't hear about it, sign anything or pay you (RCW 64.80.070).

A TOD deed can't double as a deed in lieu of foreclosure on a deed of trust (RCW 64.80.020).

What you can still do as owner

Sell it, mortgage it, rent it, live in it. The deed leaves your rights and any co-owner's rights as they were (RCW 64.80.090). The named person holds no legal or equitable stake while you live, and that person's creditors can't reach the house. Your creditors keep every claim they had, whether or not they have seen the deed. Neither your benefits eligibility nor the beneficiary's changes because of the deed.

A sale during your life wipes out the deed's effect, since only property you still own at death passes under it (RCW 64.80.100).

Canceling or replacing the deed

You can always cancel, even if the document claims it is irrevocable (RCW 64.80.030). Under RCW 64.80.080 you need a fresh recorded paper, and there are three choices:

  • A newer TOD deed that cancels the older one by name or by contradicting it.
  • A standalone revocation that says it cancels the earlier deed.
  • An ordinary lifetime deed that says it cancels the earlier deed.

Whatever you choose must carry an acknowledgment dated after the one on the deed you are canceling, and it must reach the recorder's office in the original deed's county while you are alive. Scribbling on the old deed or destroying your copy accomplishes nothing. When co-owners signed, one owner's cancellation affects only that owner's share. For community property deeded by both spouses or partners, both must cancel unless one has died.

What happens at death

The house goes to the named person only if that person is still alive when you die. A beneficiary who dies first loses the share (RCW 64.80.100). Several beneficiaries split into equal undivided shares without survivorship rights, and a dead beneficiary's share is redistributed among the rest by their existing proportions.

Situation at deathResult under RCW 64.80.100
Beneficiary outlives ownerInterest passes under the deed
Beneficiary dies firstThat beneficiary's interest lapses
Owner was a joint owner with survivorsProperty goes to the surviving joint owners by survivorship
Owner was the last surviving joint ownerThe deed takes effect
Community property, spouse did not join the deedOwner's interest passes under the deed
Community property, spouse joined and survivesThe deed is not effective at that death

Whoever inherits receives the house with its debts attached: mortgages, liens and contracts that existed at death. Liens recorded in the twenty-four months after death under RCW 41.05A.090 and 43.20B.080 count too. No warranty of title comes with the transfer, whatever the deed recites. The beneficiary can also be pulled in to cover allowed probate claims and the statutory allowances for a surviving spouse and children, within the limits of RCW 64.80.120, and can refuse the gift in whole or in part under chapter 11.86 RCW.

Real estate excise tax at death

Usually nothing is owed. WAC 458-61A-202, the Department of Revenue's inheritance rule, exempts a house passing under a TOD deed that was recorded earlier. To claim it, give the county treasurer a certified death certificate and record it with the auditor. A transfer that pays off a contract debt the owner had to the beneficiary is the exception, and tax applies.

The break doesn't follow the house to a buyer. When an heir sells, that sale is taxable under the same rule. The Department's real estate excise tax page adds that sellers typically bear the tax, payment goes to the county treasurer on the sale date, and an exemption is claimed by entering a code on the affidavit.

Other ways to pass a Washington house

Probate through a will is the main alternative. A court appoints a personal representative, and one with nonintervention powers can distribute under RCW 11.68.090 with no excise tax when nobody pays anything for the property.

The small estate affidavit in RCW 11.62.010 is a narrower shortcut. A successor uses it to collect debts and personal property owed to the estate. It applies when the probate estate is worth $100,000 or less after liens, a surviving spouse's community share is left out, and forty days must elapse after the death. Because it speaks of debts and personal property, ask a Washington attorney before relying on it for real estate.

Selling a house you inherited this way

If you received a house by TOD deed and don't want to fix it up, list it or clear it out, a cash buyer can close from the recorded deed and death certificate. Call the county auditor and a title company first and ask what must be recorded. Gather the certified death certificate and a copy of the recorded deed. A cash sale skips showings and a lender's appraisal, though the mortgage and any liens that came with the house get paid from the proceeds.

The inheritance was exempt, but your own sale is taxable. Ask the escrow officer to estimate the excise tax so your net figure is realistic.

Frequently asked questions

Must a Washington TOD deed be recorded before the owner dies?

Yes. RCW 64.80.060 says the deed has to be recorded with the county auditor where the property is located while the owner is alive. An unrecorded deed doesn't work.

Can the owner cancel a recorded TOD deed?

Yes, even if the deed says it can't be canceled. Record a newer TOD deed, a revocation or a deed that expressly cancels it, acknowledged and filed in the same county before death.

Does my beneficiary need to know about the deed?

No. The deed is valid without notice, delivery or acceptance while you are living, and the beneficiary pays nothing for it (RCW 64.80.070).

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

That person's share lapses. When several people were named, the lapsed share is divided among the others in proportion to what they hold (RCW 64.80.100).

Is excise tax owed when the house passes at the owner's death?

Generally no. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts the transfer and asks for a certified death certificate. Tax applies if the transfer pays off a contract obligation the owner owed to the beneficiary.

How probate works when a Washington homeowner dies

Probate begins when someone delivers the will to the superior court or a personal representative is appointed. It ends once debts are handled and property is distributed or sold. The personal representative is the person the court puts in charge, usually the executor named in the will.

Title 11 of the Revised Code of Washington governs the process. For a house sale, three questions matter most: who has authority to sign a deed, which creditors must be dealt with first, and whether any tax is due on the transfer.

If you inherited a house and want to sell, begin by finding out who holds authority to sign. The superior court clerk in the county where the decedent lived can tell you which filings the court expects to see.

First steps after the death

Whoever holds the original will faces a short deadline. Under RCW 11.20.010, a custodian must deliver it to the court or the named executor within thirty days of learning of the death, and an executor holding it must deliver it to the court within forty days. Someone who willfully breaks the rule can owe damages to anyone harmed.

Once the court appoints a personal representative, notice deadlines start. The representative has 20 days to serve or mail written notice of the appointment and the probate to each heir, legatee and devisee, and to each beneficiary of a nonprobate asset, whose names and addresses are reasonably known (RCW 11.28.237). Proof of service is filed with the court.

The same section requires notice to the Department of Social and Health Services office of financial recovery within 30 days of appointment, unless the representative gives creditor notice under chapter 11.40 RCW in that time.

Small estate affidavit

Sometimes an estate can skip probate. The affidavit procedure in RCW 11.62.010 lets a successor collect the decedent's personal property and debts owed to the decedent without opening a probate. It applies only when the probate estate, minus liens and encumbrances and leaving out a surviving spouse's or partner's community property interest, is $100,000 or less.

The person signing states, among other things, that:

  • at least forty days have gone by since the death;
  • the decedent lived in Washington;
  • no petition to appoint a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere;
  • all debts, including funeral and burial costs, are paid or provided for;
  • every other successor was told in writing at least ten days earlier.

A copy of the affidavit with the decedent's Social Security number goes by mail to the DSHS office of financial recovery. The procedure covers personal property and debts. If a house is part of the estate, ask the superior court clerk or an estate attorney which procedure applies to real property before you line up a buyer.

Who can sell the house, and does the court have to approve?

A personal representative with nonintervention powers can sell without returning to court. RCW 11.68.090 lets that representative mortgage, encumber, lease, sell, exchange, convey and assign the decedent's real and personal property with no court order and no notice to or approval from any court.

Duties come with the freedom. The representative acts for the benefit of everyone interested in the estate and uses discretionary powers in good faith, with honest judgment, consistent with the probated will and the beneficiaries' interests. A will can add to or limit nonintervention powers within the statute's limits.

A representative without nonintervention powers does not get that exemption from court procedures, so ask the clerk or an estate attorney which steps apply. For the excise tax paperwork on a probated estate, the Department of Revenue rule calls for a certified copy of the letters showing who the court appointed. Ask the clerk for them early.

Creditors and claim deadlines

Giving notice to creditors is optional but protective. Under RCW 11.40.020, a representative who gives notice files it with the court, publishes it once a week for three successive weeks in a legal newspaper in the county where the estate is administered, and mails a copy with the decedent's Social Security number to DSHS. A creditor who becomes known can be served by mail at any point.

RCW 11.40.051 sets claim deadlines, and a creditor's time depends on the notice given:

  • Actual notice received: the later of 30 days after mailing or four months after first publication.
  • No actual notice, creditor not reasonably ascertainable: four months after first publication.
  • No actual notice, creditor reasonably ascertainable: 24 months after the date of death.
  • No notice given at all: 24 months after the date of death.

The bar covers probate and nonprobate assets alike. Paying out sale proceeds too early can leave the representative exposed to claims that surface later, so hold back until the claim period is behind you.

Excise tax on an inherited Washington house

Passing a house to an heir does not trigger the real estate excise tax. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts transfers by devise or inheritance whether or not a mortgage is attached. A nonpro rata distribution by a personal representative is also exempt when RCW 11.68.090 authorizes it and no consideration is paid to the representative.

The exemption ends with the heir. If the heir then sells to an outside buyer, the sale is taxed on the full price. The rule's examples are blunt: someone who inherits a property and sells it for $50,000 owes tax on $50,000, and someone who sells on a real estate contract for $100,000 owes tax on $100,000. Buying out a sibling's share with cash is taxed on the amount paid.

Paperwork goes to the county treasurer and is recorded with the county auditor. For a probated will, the rule calls for a certified copy of the letters testamentary or letters of administration.

Can an heir contest the will before a sale?

Yes, within four months. RCW 11.24.010 lets any interested person petition to contest a will's validity within four months after it is admitted to probate or rejected. Filing starts the contest, but the petitioner must personally serve the personal representative within ninety days or the action is treated as never begun. If nobody files and serves in time, the probate or rejection becomes binding and final.

A house sold soon after the will is admitted can still be affected by a contest filed inside that window. Before you set a closing date, ask the estate's attorney whether the four months are over.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in Washington?

Usually the seller needs authority to sign, and that comes from a court-appointed personal representative. The small estate affidavit covers personal property and debts, so ask the superior court clerk how real property in a small estate is handled.

Can a personal representative sell without a court hearing?

Yes, if the court granted nonintervention powers. RCW 11.68.090 allows the sale of real property without a court order or notice, though the representative must still act in good faith for the beneficiaries.

How long do creditors have to file claims against an estate?

It depends on notice. A creditor with actual notice has the later of 30 days or four months after first publication, and a known creditor who got none has 24 months from the date of death under RCW 11.40.051.

Is real estate excise tax owed when an heir receives the house?

No. Transfers by inheritance or devise are exempt, but a later sale by the heir to a buyer is taxed on the full sale price.

How soon must a will be filed after death?

Whoever holds the will must deliver it to the court or the named executor within thirty days of learning of the death. An executor must get it to the court within forty days.
